title: A City of Bicycles
summary: In Copenhagen, more people go to work by bike than by car. How did the city do it?
paragraphs: Every morning in Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, thousands of people get on their bicycles and ride to work. They ride in the rain, in the snow and in the dark winter mornings. Today, about half of all trips to work or school in the city are made by bike. Many other cities around the world are trying to copy this success.

But Copenhagen was not always like this. In the 1960s and 1970s, the city was full of cars. Streets were busy and the air was dirty. Then, in 1973, oil prices suddenly rose, and petrol became very expensive. Many people could not afford to drive. The city government decided to make cycling easier and safer.

Over the next fifty years, the city built more than three hundred and eighty kilometres of bike lanes. Most of these lanes are separated from the cars by a small step, so riders feel safe. On some busy roads, traffic lights are timed for bicycles, not cars. If you ride at about twenty kilometres an hour, you will meet green lights all the way into the city centre.

The city has also built special bridges just for bicycles and people walking. One of them, called the Bicycle Snake, is an orange bridge that curves above the water between buildings. There are bike parking areas at every train station, and you can take your bicycle on the train for free.

Interestingly, most people in Copenhagen do not cycle because they want to protect the environment. When asked, the majority say they cycle simply because it is the fastest and easiest way to get around. It is also cheap, and it keeps them fit.

The benefits for the city are huge. There is less traffic and less noise. The air is cleaner. Experts say that every kilometre someone cycles instead of drives saves the country money, because people are healthier and need less medical care.

Of course, not everyone is happy. Some drivers complain that there is not enough space for cars. And on busy mornings, the bike lanes can have traffic jams of their own. But for most people in Copenhagen, life without bicycles is impossible to imagine.

questions.question: What made the city start supporting cycling in 1973?
options: A new mayor who loved bikes
questions.explanation: In 1973 oil prices rose and petrol became very expensive, so the city made cycling easier.

questions.question: How are most bike lanes separated from cars?
questions.explanation: Most lanes are separated from the cars by a small step.

questions.question: What happens if you ride at about twenty kilometres an hour on some roads?
options: You meet green lights all the way
You can ride on the train
questions.explanation: Traffic lights are timed so that at twenty km/h you meet green lights all the way.

questions.question: Why do most people in Copenhagen cycle?
options: Because it is the fastest and easiest way
questions.explanation: Most say they cycle because it is the fastest and easiest way to get around.

questions.question: Which problem with cycling is mentioned?
options: Bike lanes can have traffic jams
questions.explanation: On busy mornings, bike lanes can have traffic jams of their own.

grammar.explanation: If + present, will + verb can describe what happens when a condition is true.
grammar.example: If you ride at about twenty kilometres an hour, you will meet green lights all the way into the city centre.
